title: Building agent fleet architectures your CISO doesn't hate — Lou Bichard, Gitpod
talk_summary: Lou Bichard of Gitpod recounts how they moved from multi-tenant Kubernetes SaaS to self-hosted, then to a lightweight 'runner' (a single ECS task) that runs inside the customer's cloud, keeping source code and data on customer infrastructure while metadata stays with the vendor. They then reused that same runner/dev-environment substrate to run their AI agent fleet, inheriting the same access, privileges, and audit logging as human developers.

takeaways.technique: Thin runner inside customer/own infra instead of heavyweight orchestration
takeaways.what_they_do: Replace Kubernetes-based multi-tenant orchestration with a minimal runner (a single container/ECS task) that executes workloads on the underlying cloud primitives (EC2/EBS), inheriting native features rather than portability layers.
takeaways.numbers: runner costs single-digit dollars/month; setup as little as 3 minutes

takeaways.technique: Split sensitive workload from vendor-side metadata
takeaways.what_they_do: Keep source code, data, and integrations on the customer's infrastructure; keep only non-sensitive metadata (user IDs, telemetry) on the vendor side.

takeaways.technique: Reuse human dev-environment substrate for agents
takeaways.what_they_do: Run agents in the exact same dev environment humans use, so they get identical source access, internal system access, and privileges without building a separate agent stack.
takeaways.evidence_quote: everything that an autonomous agent needs to operate is exactly the same thing that a dev does

takeaways.technique: API-first with full audit logging of every action
takeaways.what_they_do: Build the platform API-first so every interaction (spinning up environments, agent tasks) is audit logged, giving a complete history.
takeaways.evidence_quote: every action interaction when you spin up a dev environment And everything that you do is then audit logged
